title: Practice Set JA2 — groupBy Mechanics: One Key, Many Keys
description: Recognition track: read aggregation snippets and reason about row counts, multiple-aggregate output shape, the cost of duplicated groupBys, and the right granularity. The bugs in this module run without errors and produce plausible-looking output — they are caught by careful reading, not by the runtime.

datasets.description: Shared NordGrid meter readings — 14 distinct (region, customer_type) combinations actually present in the 20-row sample (out of 5×4 theoretically possible).

description.context: Multi-column `groupBy` produces one row per DISTINCT combination of the grouping columns that ACTUALLY APPEARS in the data — not the Cartesian product of cardinalities, and not the source row count. PySpark also treats `null` as a valid grouping value, so combinations where a grouping column is null still get their own group rather than being dropped. To predict the row count, count the distinct combinations present (including nulls), not the theoretical cross-product.

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: 20 rows. region: NORTH/SOUTH/EAST/WEST + 2 null rows. customer_type: RESIDENTIAL/COMMERCIAL/INDUSTRIAL + 3 null rows. Distinct (region, customer_type) pairs ACTUALLY present in the data: 14.

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum

result = df.groupBy('region', 'customer_type').agg(sum('daily_kw'))
print(result.count())

fields.label: What number does `print()` output?
options: 20 — groupBy preserves every input row and just attaches a sum column to each, so the result has the same row count as the source DataFrame.
12 — Cartesian product of grouping-column cardinalities, 4 regions × 3 customer_types, gives 12 possible combinations and groupBy emits all of them.
14 — one row per distinct (region, customer_type) combination ACTUALLY present in the data, including pairs where either column is null (treated as a group like any other).
9 — the count of non-null distinct combinations only; PySpark follows SQL's GROUP BY convention and drops any group whose key contains a null.
fields.correctAnswer: 14 — one row per distinct (region, customer_type) combination ACTUALLY present in the data, including pairs where either column is null (treated as a group like any other).
fields.rationale: Multi-column groupBy emits one row per distinct combination that appears in the actual data — not the Cartesian product (12), not the source row.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats groupBy as if it preserved input rows; groupBy collapses rows that share the grouping key into one row per group.

description.context: PySpark has two ways to sum 'only NORTH rows': filter the DataFrame first, OR use a conditional expression inside `sum(when(...))`. Both produce the same number, but the work is different. `.filter()` is a NARROW transformation applied during the file scan — non-matching rows never reach the aggregation. `sum(when(...).otherwise(0))` evaluates the expression on every row of the input, contributing zero for non-NORTH rows but still touching them. Catalyst does NOT rewrite one form into the other because the semantics differ subtly (e.g., what `otherwise(0)` does to nulls).
description.task: Which snippet is faster on the full 500K-row dataset, and why?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Production: 500K rows; NORTH ~25% of them. Both snippets produce identical output.

evidence.label: Snippet A — conditional inside the aggregate
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum, when, col

result_a = df.agg(
    sum(when(col('region') == 'NORTH', col('daily_kw')).otherwise(0))
)

evidence.label: Snippet B — filter first, then aggregate
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum, col

result_b = (df
    .filter(col('region') == 'NORTH')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw')))

fields.label: Which snippet is faster on the full 500K-row dataset, and why?
options: Snippet A is faster — keeping the conditional inside the aggregate avoids a separate filter pass; Spark fuses the predicate into the aggregate evaluation in one efficient scan.
Snippet B is faster — `.filter()` is narrow and applied during the file scan, so only ~25% of rows reach the aggregator; Snippet A evaluates the conditional on every one of the 500K rows.
Both are equally fast — Catalyst recognises that `sum(when(...))` is semantically equivalent to filter+sum and rewrites Snippet A into Snippet B's plan during optimization.
Snippet A is faster because filter triggers a shuffle to redistribute non-matching rows; Snippet A keeps the data in place and avoids the network cost entirely.
fields.correctAnswer: Snippet B is faster — `.filter()` is narrow and applied during the file scan, so only ~25% of rows reach the aggregator; Snippet A evaluates the conditional on every one of the 500K rows.
fields.rationale: `.filter()` is a narrow transformation pushed into the scan, so non-NORTH rows are dropped before any aggregation work happens — Snippet B operates.
fields.distractorRationale: filter()` as a separate pass; in Spark, filter is narrow and fused into the scan that the aggregation already needs.

description.context: Stacking multiple aggregates inside a single `.agg(...)` call computes all of them in ONE shuffle pass. Splitting them across separate `.groupBy(...).agg(...)` calls and then joining the results triggers MULTIPLE shuffles — one per groupBy plus a third shuffle (or broadcast) for the join. Catalyst optimizes within a single logical plan but does NOT detect that two separately-built DataFrames share the same groupBy operation; they appear as independent subtrees.
description.task: Which snippet is faster, and what mechanism causes the difference?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Both snippets produce identical (region, total_kw, avg_kw) output. Question is shuffle count.

evidence.label: Snippet A — two aggregations joined back together
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum, avg

sums = df.groupBy('region').agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'))
avgs = df.groupBy('region').agg(avg('daily_kw').alias('avg_kw'))
result_a = sums.join(avgs, on='region', how='inner')

evidence.label: Snippet B — both aggregates in a single .agg()
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum, avg

result_b = df.groupBy('region').agg(
    sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw'),
    avg('daily_kw').alias('avg_kw')
)

fields.label: Which snippet is faster, and what mechanism causes the difference?
options: Snippet A is faster — splitting sum and avg into two separate jobs gives Spark more parallelism because the two aggregations run on independent executor groups in parallel.
Both are equivalent in cost — Catalyst detects that the two groupBy calls operate on the same DataFrame and merges them into a single plan, so the physical plans become identical.
Snippet B is faster — stacked aggregates share ONE shuffle by region. Snippet A shuffles twice (one per groupBy) plus a third operation for the join, multiplying shuffle cost.
Snippet B is faster only on small data; on large data the join in Snippet A becomes a broadcast hash join and removes the duplicated shuffle, making both snippets equivalent at scale.
fields.correctAnswer: Snippet B is faster — stacked aggregates share ONE shuffle by region. Snippet A shuffles twice (one per groupBy) plus a third operation for the join, multiplying shuffle cost.
fields.rationale: Snippet B triggers exactly one shuffle by region; both aggregates compute in that one pass.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Believes more jobs means more parallelism; Spark parallelizes within each shuffle across all executors, so splitting just adds overhead.

description.context: The granularity of a `groupBy` result is determined ENTIRELY by the columns passed as grouping keys — not by the alias on the aggregate, not by the comment above the code. If the date column carries DAILY values like `2026-03-01`, then `groupBy('region', 'date')` produces one row per (region, daily-date) pair — daily granularity, not monthly. To roll up to month, you must TRANSFORM the date first: `groupBy('region', month('date'))` or `date_trunc('month', col('date'))`. This class of bug is silent — every row has correct values, only the row COUNT is wrong.
description.task: Which line contains the bug, and what is the underlying mechanism?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content: Code spec: 'monthly regional consumption' (4 regions × 3 months = 12 rows expected). Actual output: hundreds of rows, each with a correct total_kw for its (region, date).

evidence.label: snippet.py
evidence.content:
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum

# Compute monthly consumption per region
monthly_regional = (df
    .groupBy('region', 'date')
    .agg(sum('daily_kw').alias('total_kw')))

monthly_regional.write.mode('overwrite').parquet('gold/monthly_regional')

fields.label: Which line contains the bug, and what is the underlying mechanism?
options: Line 5: `groupBy('region', 'date')` groups by DAILY date because the column carries daily values; the result has daily granularity, not monthly. Fix: transform with `month('date')` or `date_trunc('month', col('date'))` before grouping.

Line 6: `.alias('total_kw')` is wrong — the output column should be named `monthly_total_kw` to signal the intended monthly granularity to downstream consumers; the alias is the source of the granularity confusion.

Line 8: `write.mode('overwrite')` is silently appending instead of replacing, so rows from previous daily runs accumulate; the fix is to delete the path before each write to ensure clean monthly output.
There is no bug — the dashboard team should aggregate further at the BI layer; producing daily granularity from this pipeline is correct because it gives consumers maximum flexibility.
fields.correctAnswer: Line 5: `groupBy('region', 'date')` groups by DAILY date because the column carries daily values; the result has daily granularity, not monthly. Fix: transform with `month('date')` or `date_trunc('month', col('date'))` before grouping.
fields.rationale: groupBy granularity is determined by the values in the grouping columns.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Treats column names as the source of granularity; aliasing the output column does not change row count, only the groupBy keys do.
